claims.text: Pulumi's component state migrations let component authors evolve a reusable Pulumi component's internal design and ship the upgrade path (a state migration) in the same release as the component code, preserving existing infrastructure.
Component state migrations are new in Pulumi.
A Pulumi component state migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change.
The Pulumi component state migrations API is experimental and may change.
A GitHub discussion for component state migrations feedback exists at https://github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ and covers the component state migration callback contract.
The pulumi/examples repository contains an example at aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration containing all three programs (v1, v2, v3) and the migration code.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/concepts/components/ describing components.

The first version (v1) of the example uses the legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component, which creates a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway, with a security group outside the component that refers to the VPC.
Replacing an AWS VPC means the security group that refers to the VPC's ID must also be replaced, per the AWS CloudFormation EC2 SecurityGroup VpcId property documentation.
Without a migration connecting the old state to the new code, upgrading from the legacy AWSX VPC component to the modern one could replace the VPC instead of keeping it.
The example does not create a database.
If a database is recreated, its replacement does not automatically contain the old data, and without a backup or data migration deleting the old database could mean losing that data.
The second version (v2) of the example upgrades to the modern `awsx.ec2.Vpc` component while keeping the existing network.
The third version (v3) of the example removes AWSX and declares the VPC, subnet, route table, route table association, and internet gateway directly with `@pulumi/aws`.
Across all three versions of the example, the AWS resource IDs stay the same and the security group continues to use the same VPC.

In the v1 example the Pulumi state tree is: `awsx:x:ec2:Vpc` "vpc" containing `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc`, an `awsx:x:ec2:Subnet` "vpc-isolated-0" (containing Subnet, RouteTable, RouteTableAssociation), and an `awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway` "vpc" (containing an InternetGateway).

In the v2 example the Pulumi state tree is: `awsx:ec2:Vpc` "vpc" containing `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc` "vpc", with subnet "vpc-isolated-1" (with route table and association nested beneath it) and internet gateway "vpc" as children of the managed VPC.

In the v3 example the Pulumi state tree has `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc` "vpc" as root, with subnet "vpc-isolated-1" (route table and association nested) and internet gateway "vpc" beneath it, with no `awsx:` component records.

Pulumi state records both physical resources and the components that group them; each record has a Pulumi name called a URN, and managed resources also have an ID from the cloud provider such as an AWS VPC ID.
The legacy AWSX VPC component wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components, while modern AWSX removes those wrappers and puts the managed resources under different parents.
In the example, the Pulumi name of the subnet changes from `vpc-isolated-0` to `vpc-isolated-1` when moving from legacy to modern AWSX.
Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible.

The legacy-to-modern AWSX upgrade needs to remove component wrappers and transfer references to the replacement resources, which aliases alone do not handle; a state migration describes that whole change together.
A Pulumi component registers a migration callback through the `stateMigrations` resource option, together with an alias for the legacy component type.
`migrateClassicVpc` comes from the example's v2/migration.ts file at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/blob/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts.
With a component state migration, the alias lets Pulumi find the old component, and the migration callback receives the old component's saved state followed by the state of its children.

A Pulumi state migration callback returns two things: `newState` (the complete set of records that should replace the old component and its children) and `successors` (a map from each old URN that disappears to the URN that takes its place).
The example's migration callback is safe to run again: if state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources it does nothing, and an unexpected component type raises an error instead of guessing.
The example's `rename` helper copies the saved record and changes its URN, type, and parent, preserving the AWS resource ID and other saved fields, and moves the subnet under the managed VPC.

The `successors` map entries let the Pulumi engine know that the old component wrapper and the managed subnet point to the same new subnet record; Pulumi uses these mappings to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack.
In the example, the VPC successor mapping keeps the security group's reference to the VPC connected to the migrated VPC record, which retains the same AWS VPC ID.
The v3 migration changes who defines the resources in the program; users can then adjust their configuration in a separate update.

The second migration (v3/migration.ts) removes the AWSX VPC component record and moves the managed VPC into its place; both the old component and its VPC child map to the new VPC record, the VPC keeps its AWS ID, and the other resources remain beneath it.
The second migration is at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/blob/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v3/migration.ts.
In the example's v3 program, the VPC registration keeps aliases for both previous component types (legacy and modern AWSX VPC) and both migration callbacks.
When a component registers multiple state migration callbacks, Pulumi runs the callbacks in order, passing each result to the next callback.
With the example's two migrations, a stack still using legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to the plain AWS version, and a stack already using modern AWSX skips the first migration.
Once both migrations have run, both callbacks return no result on later updates.
Keeping earlier migrations with the component means users can skip versions without editing stack state by hand.
After a state migration changes saved state, Pulumi compares the new program with that state and calls the provider for any remaining changes.
Keeping resource IDs does not mean every upgrade has an empty preview: the example can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags.
To try the example, start with `v1` and follow its README, using the same stack, backend, project name, AWS region, and availability zone for each version.
When upgrading the example, `pulumi preview` should show no creates, deletes, or replacements for the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group.
`pulumi preview` evaluates the state migration without saving it, and `pulumi up` saves the migrated state.

When a component author registers a state migration inside the component implementation, users do not need to write the migration, attach the callback, or edit their stack state; Pulumi runs the migration as part of the normal preview and update after they upgrade the component.
For an internal component change that keeps the same inputs and outputs, users can keep their existing component calls without needing to know which resources moved or how the saved state changed.
Pulumi state migration callbacks (the resource option documented on the state migrations resource-options page) run during both previews and updates when prior state exists for the resource.
Pulumi state migration callbacks must be idempotent and must return no result when the state no longer needs migration.
Pulumi state migration callbacks rewrite resource state without performing provider operations.

A Pulumi component state migration (the `stateMigrations` resource option callback) is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A Pulumi component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings.
In a Pulumi component state migration result, each successor mapping connects an old URN that is omitted from the returned result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, a Pulumi component state migration callback returns no result.
A Pulumi component state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached to a component when using update plans or targeted updates.
The Pulumi restrictions on state-changing results of component state migrations (when using update plans or targeted updates) do not require removing an already-applied migration.
The Pulumi component state migration callback's state entries use the checkpoint resource format, including fields such as `urn`, `type`, `id`, `parent`, `provider`, `inputs`, and `outputs`.
